idiom_name: Flipper.enabled? with actors, groups and percentage rollout
implementation_notes: Flipper is the dominant Ruby realization of the complete structure: Flipper.enabled?(:search, current_user) is the toggle router call, enable_actor / enable_group / enable_percentage_of_actors are the toggle-context strategies, and an adapter (memory, ActiveRecord, Redis, ...) is the state repository, so application code never reaches for the flag store itself. Without the gem the pattern degenerates to ENV['FF_NEW_CHECKOUT'] == '1' read once at boot, which is enough for a process-wide release flag but has no targeting, no per-actor consistency and no history of who flipped what. The full structure is justified exactly when flags are rolled out gradually or administered by non-developers; for a handful of release flags the environment variable is the honest implementation.
code_sketch:
# toggle point
if Flipper.enabled?(:new_checkout, current_user)
  new_checkout(cart)
else
  legacy_checkout(cart)
end

# progressive rollout
Flipper.enable_percentage_of_actors :new_checkout, 2
Flipper.enable_group :new_checkout, :beta_testers
pitfalls: A percentage rollout without an actor argument falls back to a per-process random value, so the same user flips between branches from request to request.
The memory adapter starts every flag off in each new process and forgets flips on restart: state that must survive a deploy has to be persisted (ActiveRecord, Redis) up front.
Gates left in the code after rollout keep the gem's check and the flag's registration in every request; remove the gate once a feature is permanent.
Flipper reads the local adapter on every check - a remote/cloud adapter is synced in the background, so a flip is not instantaneous across a fleet.
